name: Sauna

lead: A sauna is a room heated to roughly 70-105 C with low humidity, where you sit and sweat. People in appearance communities use it to look less puffy in the face, recover between training sessions and sleep better, and some say it raises growth hormone.

Heat causes sweating, wider blood vessels and a raised heart rate, a load similar to light exercise. The recovery and relaxation that follow are what users tie to a fresher face and better gains. Published research is mostly about heart and circulation health: a Finnish cohort linked frequent sauna bathing with lower cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, and small trials report improved vascular function. No studies have looked at facial appearance, and a purported study of brow-ridge bone growth that circulates on forums does not appear in the literature.

paras: People use traditional, electric, steam or infrared saunas, often after a workout or in the evening, in sessions of a few rounds with cooling breaks in between. It is commonly paired with hydration, sleep routines and training schedules. Effects on puffiness and relaxation are usually felt the same day, while the cardiovascular research concerns regular use over years.

Alcohol, dehydration and certain heart conditions such as unstable angina or severe aortic stenosis raise risk, and pregnancy calls for limits on core temperature. Rapid sweat-based weight loss, as practised in combat sports, has documented physiological effects. People with heart or blood pressure conditions are generally advised to check with a clinician first.

angle.text: Heat exposure and sweating relax you and help recovery, which users link to a less puffy face and better training gains, and some to higher growth hormone. Finnish cohorts have studied sauna for heart health; the facial and bone claims have not been studied.

lead: A sauna is a room or building heated to high temperatures, traditionally 70 to 105 C in the Finnish style with low humidity, where people sit to sweat, often adding bursts of steam by pouring water on hot stones [1][2]. Variants include the wood-fired and smoke sauna, the electric sauna, steam rooms and hammams, and infrared cabins that warm the body at lower air temperatures of roughly 40 to 60 C [1][3].

In looksmaxxing and wider fitness communities the sauna is used as a low-cost routine: after training for recovery and relaxation, and before a photo or event for a temporarily leaner, less puffy look that users attribute to sweat and fluid loss [4][5][6]. Some users also repeat claims that heat raises growth hormone, and one thread circulates a purported study of brow-ridge bone growth from an institute that does not appear in the published literature [7][8][9].

Published research centres on cardiovascular outcomes. A Finnish prospective cohort of middle-aged men linked more frequent sauna bathing to lower rates of sudden cardiac death, fatal cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality [10], and small interventional trials report improved vascular function after repeated heat exposure [11][12][13]. Reviews also describe risks, including alcohol, dehydration and certain heart conditions [14][1]. No published trial has examined sauna use for facial puffiness, bone or growth hormone as an appearance intervention.
infobox: Heated bathing room (dry, wet or infrared)
About 70-105 C Finnish style; spa settings often 70-80 C; infrared cabins about 40-60 C [1][3]
Võromaa smoke sauna UNESCO-listed 2014; Finnish sauna culture 2020 [1]

paras: Traditional Finnish saunas are typically heated to about 75 to 100 C, sometimes higher, and a defining feature is löyly, the steam released when water meets hot stones [1][2]. Bathers control the heat through water on the stove, session length and bench height, since heat rises and higher benches are hotter [1]. Smoke saunas lack a chimney and are heated for six to eight hours before use, with heat lasting up to twelve; electric stoves, the most common modern type, warm a room in roughly 15 to 30 minutes [1]. Heat-storage stoves use sealed stone compartments and give a softer, cleaner heat [1]. Steam baths such as the hammam run near full humidity at about 50 C [1].

Infrared saunas use heaters that emit far-infrared light, absorbed by the skin as radiant heat, so they run at roughly 40 to 60 C air temperature compared with 70 to 90 C for a traditional sauna [3]. Designs range from cabins to cheaper tent-like units [3]. Wikipedia reports that a 2009 review found limited evidence for effects on blood pressure and congestive heart failure in infrared users, that the studies were small and short, and that the liver and kidneys carry out detoxification, with sweat removing a negligible amount of toxins [3].

Heated bathing is ancient and widespread. Wikipedia mentions possible steam use in Neolithic stone structures on Scotland's Orkney Islands from about 4000 BCE, Korean hanjeungmak recorded in the fifteenth-century Sejong Sillok, and the Roman thermae, Turkish hammam, Mesoamerican temazcal, Russian banya, Japanese mushi-buro, Korean jjimjilbang and Native American sweat lodges, the last of which are spiritual ceremonies rather than recreation [1].

The earliest Finnish saunas were pit dwellings, followed by smoke saunas; in the Industrial Revolution metal wood-burning stoves with chimneys (kiuas) became common [1]. Metos Ltd of Vaasa introduced the electric sauna stove in 1938 [1]. A Finnish sauna in the Finnish team's quarters drew attention at the 1936 Berlin Olympics, and Viherjuuri's Sauna Book appeared in 1941 [1]. After the Second World War, German soldiers who had used saunas during the Continuation War carried the custom to Germany and Austria [1]. UNESCO listed the Võromaa smoke sauna tradition in 2014 and Finnish sauna culture in 2020 [1]. In the United States sauna culture is tied to Finnish-American communities in the Upper Midwest, and Duluth once had 14 public saunas [1]. John Harvey Kellogg's 1891 radiant heat bath is cited as an ancestor of infrared saunas [3].

Sitting in a sauna produces mild hyperthermia, with sweating, vasodilation and a raised heart rate [2][14]. A 2021 review in Experimental Gerontology describes a thermoregulatory response involving neuroendocrine, cardiovascular and cytoprotective mechanisms, and proposes that repeated sessions acclimate the body to heat through hormesis, the pattern in which a mild stressor prompts adaptive responses [15]. Wikipedia says heat stress may activate heat-shock proteins [1].

A medical review states that sauna bathing causes acute, transient cardiovascular and hormonal changes and is well tolerated by most healthy adults [14]; the catecholamine response in Finnish sauna was studied as early as the 1970s [16]. The cardiovascular findings have been linked to improved endothelium-dependent dilation, reduced arterial stiffness, changes in autonomic nervous system activity and lower blood pressure [17][11][18].

The most common appearance use is a temporary reduction in water weight and puffiness. Users on looksmax.org describe looking leaner after sessions and attribute it to sweating out water [4]. A review of combat sports, where athletes use heat and sweat-based fluid loss to make weight, describes the physiological effects of that fluid loss [19]. No published study has measured facial puffiness after sauna use.
A medical review reports that sauna bathing does not cause drying of the skin and may benefit patients with psoriasis, while sweating may increase itching in atopic dermatitis [14].

Sauna use after training is common in lifting communities; T Nation training logs list sauna time on conditioning and regeneration days [20]. A crossover study of six male distance runners tested three weeks of post-exercise sauna bathing against control training for its effect on a treadmill performance test [21], a randomised trial in 47 low-active adults compared exercise combined with sauna bathing against exercise alone for cardiovascular function [22], and a 2025 trial reported that regular post-exercise sauna bathing did not improve heart rate variability [23].

The most cited observational study is the Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease cohort in eastern Finland, published in JAMA Internal Medicine in 2015, which followed middle-aged men and reported lower risk of sudden cardiac death, fatal coronary and cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality among men with more frequent sauna sessions and longer durations [10]. A 2018 Mayo Clinic Proceedings review summarised epidemiological and interventional work linking sauna bathing to lower risk of high blood pressure, cardiovascular and neurocognitive disease, pulmonary disease and mortality, with proposed mechanisms in endothelial function, arterial stiffness and the autonomic nervous system [17]. The 2021 healthspan review also describes dose-dependent links in prospective cohorts [15]. Observational associations cannot establish causation.

Interventional studies are smaller. Repeated sauna or thermal therapy was reported to improve vascular endothelial function in patients with coronary risk factors and in chronic heart failure, and a single thermal vasodilation session produced acute haemodynamic improvement in heart failure [12][13][24]. An eight-week study of repeated hot-water immersion in sedentary young adults reported improved endothelial function, arterial stiffness and blood pressure compared with thermoneutral immersion, testing water immersion rather than a sauna [11]. A 2021 Journal of Applied Physiology review covers the mechanisms of heat therapy [18]. A randomised trial of combined spa and exercise therapy reported benefit in ankylosing spondylitis [25]. A feasibility trial studied a whole-body hyperthermia protocol [26], and a German-language review assessed the potential of sauna in prevention [27].
No published human trials were found that test sauna use for facial puffiness, brow-ridge bone or growth hormone as an appearance intervention.

Reviews note that alcohol, dehydration and narcotics increase the risk of sudden death in saunas, that unstable angina, recent myocardial infarction and severe aortic stenosis are contraindications, and that people with severe obesity, high blood pressure or diabetes are advised shorter sessions [1][14]. Pregnancy guidance is to keep core temperature below about 39 C [1]; a 1992 JAMA study linked maternal heat exposure to neural tube defects [28]. A case report describes fatal rhabdomyolysis associated with sauna use [29]. A medical review states that sauna bathing does not influence fertility, while a study of genital heat stress reported effects on semen quality [14][30].

The World Sauna Championships were held in Heinola, Finland, from 1999 to 2010, starting at 110 C; after the 7 August 2010 final two competitors were pulled out in critical condition and one died, and in April 2011 the city said it would no longer organise the event [31].

Sauna use has grown beyond Finland as a wellness practice, and a 2018 review notes it is becoming increasingly popular in many other populations [17]. A 2026 Hacker News thread on the effect of sauna on heart rate drew 448 points and 236 comments [32].

Members of looksmax.org discuss sauna as a debloating habit, as a recovery companion to training and cold showers, and as a possible hormone booster [4][5][9][8]. A thread titled 'sauna maxing 2022 full guide' uses the community's 'gtfih' tag, a call to get in and try the routine [33]. The brow-ridge thread quotes a study attributed to an institute and a researcher who do not appear in the published literature; replies include jokes about entering as a 'subhuman' and leaving as a 'chad' [7]. In the growth-hormone thread the original poster says a podcast host's claim led them to look for a study, and one reply says gym steam-room visits brought 'insane gains' [8].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sauna is discussed as a low-cost routine for debloating, recovery and hormones, alongside a thread presenting a purported study on bone growth [7][8][4]. In the wider lifting scene it appears in training logs as regeneration work [20].
